description:
Background As humanity aims for space missions such as BAS and lunar missions, real-time ground support becomes impossible due to communication delays. An AI-based HAR system acts as an on-board assistant that supports the execution of scientific experiments, ensuring the success of science beyond Earth's orbit.
In the space environment, AI-based HAR system may act as mission-critical support for astronauts. By tracking astronaut movements and activities in real time, HAR ensures scientific experiments and related protocols are executed flawlessly without requiring constant, high-bandwidth communication with mission control.
Description Challenge is to design and train an AI model that recognizes and validates the sequence of a pre-defined experiment using human activity recognition techniques.
Standalone operation: Space stations operate on restricted data bandwidth to Earth. Rather than streaming raw video to ground control, data is processed locally at the 'edge.' Inputs are given from fixed-payload cameras.
Dataset generation to train model for object detection, pose estimation and hand-object interaction based on the steps of the experiment.
Optional: Another challenge is that Standard 2D or ground-based 3D posture models fail because astronauts do not have a fixed 'up' or 'down' orientation. The AI model should use orientation-agnostic 3D Human Mesh Recovery (HMR) to track the astronaut’s body relative to the payload rack, not the floor.
Expected Solution
• The software should continuously process local video feeds to track the sequence of experiment.
• At the start or after each step, the model should suggest the next step to be performed.
• It should alert when a step is skipped or an out of sequence step is added. It should be a voice based alert.
• Using the live video, it should generate a timestamped and structured lightweight text file of the conducted steps with outcomes/ status.
• Stream the video of the experiment to specific IP and also store the video locally.
• A graphical user interface for monitoring the above activities.
• Deliverable: A trained AI model that runs on offline standalone system
summary: Innovation (3/5): draws on ai applied to a miscellaneous problem, placing it in the moderate band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Miscellaneous. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on model, real-time, standard. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 18/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: AI Human Activity Recognition for On-board BAS Experiments

overview.in_plain_terms: Build an AI watchdog that watches an astronaut perform a scientific experiment step by step, using onboard cameras, and flags out loud if they skip a step or do things out of order, all without needing to talk to Earth.
overview.why_it_matters: In space missions, real-time ground support is impossible because of communication delays, so an onboard AI assistant that tracks experiment execution becomes mission-critical support, catching a missed or wrong step before it wastes a limited, expensive experiment run.
pain_points: No real-time ground support means errors in experiment execution can't be caught by mission control as they happen.
Standard pose-estimation models assume a fixed 'up/down' orientation, which doesn't hold for an astronaut in microgravity.
Bandwidth to Earth is restricted, so raw video streaming isn't the answer, everything has to be processed locally on the edge.
overview.background: As missions like BAS and lunar exploration push further from Earth, communication delays make real-time ground support impossible. An AI-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR) system is proposed as an onboard assistant, tracking astronaut movements and validating experiment protocols in real time, without needing constant high-bandwidth contact with mission control.
overview.whats_being_asked: An AI model that recognizes and validates the sequence of a predefined experiment using human activity recognition, processing data locally at the edge from fixed-payload cameras, with an optional orientation-agnostic 3D Human Mesh Recovery approach since astronauts have no fixed 'up' or 'down'.
expected_solution: Continuous local video processing to track the sequence of the experiment.
At the start of or after each step, the model suggests the next step to be performed.
Voice-based alert when a step is skipped or performed out of sequence.
A timestamped, structured lightweight text log of conducted steps with outcomes/status, generated from the live video.
Streaming and local storage of the experiment video to a specific IP.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Moderate band, and the score is right, this is applied HAR (a known technique) to a novel and constrained environment, not a new ML method. The genuinely hard, differentiating part is the optional orientation-agnostic 3D Human Mesh Recovery, most teams will skip that and stick to 2D, which is the safe, defensible call given the timeline.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. You need dataset generation for a specific unseen experiment sequence, a sequence-validation model, voice-alert logic, and a structured logging pipeline, that's real breadth even before touching the microgravity orientation problem.

competitive_landscape.note: This is a specialized ISRO/space-domain PS that most general hackathon teams will avoid due to unfamiliarity with the microgravity constraint, teams comfortable with computer vision and willing to simplify the physics angle have a real edge here.

innovation.note: Sequence-validation HAR is a known ML pattern, applied to a genuinely novel operating environment (microgravity, no fixed orientation).

invention.note: Dataset creation for a custom experiment sequence, pose/action tracking, voice alerting, and structured logging together is substantial engineering.

technical_feasibility.note: You will not have real astronaut footage, plan a proxy dataset (team members simulating the experiment steps) from hour 0, that's your critical path.

impact_and_benefits.note: A missed or corrupted step in a limited, high-cost space experiment is a real, defensible failure mode this PS directly addresses.

architecture.note: Video ingestion, sequence model, alert layer, and logging form a clean pipeline, the orientation-agnostic 3D piece is the one part that could genuinely spiral in complexity if attempted.

overall_verdict.reasoning: A solid pick for a computer-vision-comfortable team that scopes down to 2D pose/action tracking on a proxy dataset rather than chasing the full orientation-agnostic 3D Human Mesh Recovery in 36 hours, that optional stretch goal is explicitly optional for a reason.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: The Expected Solution is unusually concrete: sequence tracking, voice alerts on deviation, and a structured log are all clearly demoable, testable deliverables.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: No real astronaut or microgravity footage exists for you to train or test on, if you don't build a credible proxy dataset (team members performing a mock experiment) early, you'll have nothing to demo with.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm hour 0: define your own mock 'experiment' with a fixed sequence of 4-6 steps, and start recording proxy video immediately, this dataset is your single biggest dependency.

idea_0_4: Define a simple mock experiment sequence (e.g., 5 steps: open container, pick up tool, perform action, record reading, close container) and start recording team members performing it, correctly and with deliberate errors.
Decide scope explicitly: 2D pose/action tracking only, skip the orientation-agnostic 3D HMR stretch goal unless the team has spare capacity later.
Assign owners: one person on the vision/sequence model, one on voice-alert logic, one on the logging pipeline.
prototype_4_22: Build a pose/action recognition pipeline (e.g., MediaPipe or a lightweight action-classification model) against your proxy dataset, correct-sequence detection first.
Add the deviation detector: compare the observed step sequence against the expected sequence, flag skips and out-of-order steps.
Build the voice-alert trigger and the structured timestamped log output in parallel.
integration_22_30: Wire the full loop: live/recorded video -> pose tracking -> sequence validation -> voice alert + log entry, test against your proxy recordings including the deliberate-error clips.
Add the 'suggest next step' output at the start/after each detected step.
Verify the log file format is clean and readable, this is a deliverable judges will actually open and check.
polish_30_36: Rehearse a live demo: someone performs the mock experiment on stage, including one deliberate error, and the system catches it out loud.
If time allows, add a brief proof-of-concept clip showing the orientation-agnostic angle conceptually (e.g., tracking relative to a marked rig instead of the floor), even if not fully solved.
Prepare the structured log output as a visible artifact to hand to judges.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Perform the mock experiment live on stage with a deliberate mistake built into the sequence, and let the system's voice alert catch it in real time. That live catch is more convincing than any slide.

strengths: Concrete, testable success criteria (does it catch the deliberate error or not) make for a strong live demo.
No dependency on real space hardware, a proxy dataset built from team members is a legitimate, defensible substitute.
weaknesses: No real microgravity or astronaut data exists to validate against, everything is necessarily a simulation.
The optional orientation-agnostic 3D piece is genuinely hard and easy to either skip entirely or half-build ineffectively.

roles_needed: Someone to act as the 'astronaut' for proxy data collection
team_fit.ideal_ratio: 2 CV-focused to 1 backend-focused, the core difficulty here is in the vision/sequence pipeline, not the surrounding infrastructure.
team_fit.approach: Record your proxy dataset in the first hour with multiple team members and multiple deliberate-error variants, so the model has enough variation to actually validate against by hour 20.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Boilerplate for video ingestion, MediaPipe/pose-model integration, and the logging pipeline can all be scaffolded quickly with AI assistance.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Deciding what counts as a 'step deviation' versus normal execution variance needs human judgment and iteration against your specific proxy dataset, this isn't a solved, off-the-shelf classification problem.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-suggested generic action-recognition model that was never tuned against your actual mock-experiment footage will likely misfire on both false positives and missed deviations, test against your own recordings early and often.

data_resource_availability.status: No real astronaut/microgravity dataset is publicly available for this specific use case, this is expected, the PS is written assuming teams will build a proxy demonstration.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If your proxy dataset proves too small or inconsistent, lean on synthetic augmentation (multiple camera angles, lighting variation) of your recorded clips rather than trying to gather more footage under time pressure.

judge_qna.question: You don't have real astronaut footage, how do you know this would actually work in space?
judge_qna.strong_answer: We built a proxy demonstration using a defined experiment sequence and team members performing it, which validates the core pipeline logic; the microgravity orientation problem is the genuinely unsolved piece we've scoped as a stretch goal, not pretended to solve.
judge_qna.follow_up: What would change architecturally if you had access to real microgravity footage?

judge_qna.question: How does the system tell the difference between a genuine step skip and just a slower, valid execution?
judge_qna.strong_answer: We track completion of key sub-actions within each step rather than rigid timing, so slower execution doesn't trigger a false alert, only actually skipped or reordered actions do.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your false-positive rate on your proxy dataset when execution speed varies?

judge_qna.question: Why voice alerts specifically, instead of a visual dashboard?
judge_qna.strong_answer: An astronaut mid-experiment is hands-occupied and eyes-on-task, a voice alert doesn't require looking away from the work, which matches the real operational constraint.
judge_qna.follow_up: How do you avoid the voice alert being a distraction during a delicate step?
